fields.description_1:
Tenbrugge needed a website that could make several financial services understandable without forcing visitors to learn accounting language first. Business owners and private clients may arrive with very different questions about administration, tax, payroll or financial guidance, so the main challenge was choosing a clear route before asking for contact.

The old portfolio wording described this too broadly and followed the same pattern as unrelated projects. For this case, the problem is more specific: visitors need to recognise their situation, see which service is relevant and understand what information comes next. The page structure also has to stay calm on mobile, where long explanations quickly become hard to scan. The case study should explain that decision clearly without inventing financial results or client outcomes.
fields.description_2:
I shaped the Tenbrugge WordPress site around the questions people bring to a financial adviser rather than around a long list of services. Accountancy, tax, payroll and wider financial guidance are separated into clear routes, with supporting information placed after the first choice instead of before it.

Contact and appointment actions remain visible when a visitor has enough context to continue. I kept the language plain and the sections short so someone can understand the offer without specialist knowledge. On smaller screens, service choices and next steps keep the same order. The portfolio story now focuses on the actual information problem and how the site solves it, instead of using generic claims about better design, stronger conversion or business growth that were never measured.

fields.description_1:
Sanatolia brings together culture, theatre and learning, so the website has to serve people who do not all arrive for the same reason. One visitor may be looking for a theatre event, while another wants a course such as drawing, folk dance, guitar, saz or creative drama.

Parents, adults and cultural visitors need to understand quickly where an activity belongs, what practical information matters and how to join or book. A simple list of everything would make the programme feel harder to explore. The portfolio text also needs to reflect Sanatolia's cultural role instead of sounding like a generic events website. The challenge was to organise a varied programme in a way that stays welcoming, readable and easy to use on both desktop and mobile.
fields.description_2:
For Sanatolia, I organised the WordPress experience around the two things visitors mainly want to do: discover cultural events and find a suitable activity or course. Theatre and programme content can stand on their own, while lessons such as drawing, folk dance, guitar, saz and creative drama remain easy to recognise.

Practical details and ticket or participation actions sit close to the activity they belong to, so visitors do not have to search through unrelated sections. The visual structure supports the cultural character of the organisation without hiding useful information behind large promotional blocks. On mobile, cards and actions keep a simple reading order. This makes the portfolio case specific to Sanatolia and its mixed cultural programme, rather than repeating a standard website story.

fields.description_1:
Werkenbijefe is built for people who are deciding whether a job and employer fit them. That means the site has to do more than display vacancies. Candidates need to move from vacancy discovery to role information, understand what working at EFE is like and know what happens when they apply.

With many open positions, the main risk is that the vacancy list becomes the whole experience while employer information and practical next steps disappear into the background. The portfolio text should therefore describe a recruitment journey, not a generic company website. The challenge was to keep vacancies easy to scan while giving candidates enough context to make a confident next move, especially on mobile where lists, filters and application actions become difficult to follow.
fields.description_2:
I structured Werkenbijefe around a direct candidate path: find a vacancy, understand the role and employer, then apply without unnecessary detours. Vacancy discovery stays prominent, but supporting content about working at EFE and development helps candidates judge whether a position suits them before opening the application flow.

The application process is presented as a clear sequence instead of an isolated form at the end of the site. Headings and labels use simple language, and mobile layouts keep vacancy cards, details and actions in a predictable order. This gives the portfolio entry a concrete recruitment story based on how the website is actually used. It avoids claiming more applications, better hiring results or stronger employer branding unless those outcomes have been measured separately.

fields.description_1:
RBMB sells building materials to customers who often need to make a technical choice before they can buy. The webshop covers products such as egaline, mortar, primers, floor coatings, plastering materials, adhesives, tools and insulation. A visitor may know the job they need to complete but not yet the exact product, quantity or preparation method.

That makes navigation and product context as important as the product grid itself. The portfolio problem should focus on helping buyers move from a building task to the right category and useful guidance, not on generic ecommerce wording. The challenge was to keep a broad catalogue practical for both experienced tradespeople and less experienced buyers, while preserving a clear path to product details, cart actions and supporting guides on mobile.
fields.description_2:
For RBMB, I organised the WooCommerce journey around real building tasks and product groups. Categories such as egaline, mortar, primer, floor coating, plastering products, adhesives, tools and insulation give buyers a direct starting point, while guides provide extra context when a product choice depends on preparation or application.

Product pages then carry the detail needed before adding an item to the cart, instead of forcing every explanation into category pages. The structure keeps shopping actions clear without removing the technical information that helps people choose. On mobile, category entry points, product cards and cart actions stay easy to scan. The portfolio story now reflects a specialist building-material webshop and its buying decisions, rather than repeating the same ecommerce template used for unrelated stores.

fields.description_1:
Enspect works with inspections where the type of check matters before a company can request the right service. The website covers SCIOS Scope 8, 10 and 12, NEN 3140 and NEN 1010 inspections, thermography and related technical support. Visitors may know they need an inspection but not understand which standard or scope applies to their installation.

The site therefore has to separate these routes without turning the first screen into a wall of technical terms. It also needs to explain what happens around an inspection, including the move from request to reporting. The portfolio problem is this decision gap: help a technical or facility contact identify the relevant inspection and continue with enough context, while keeping unsupported safety or compliance claims out of the study.
fields.description_2:
I structured Enspect so each inspection route can be understood on its own while fitting one technical service website. SCIOS scopes, NEN inspections and thermography are separated clearly, with practical explanations placed near the service rather than hidden in general company copy. Quote actions appear after enough context has been given to make the request meaningful.

The site also shows the inspection journey in a simple order, from choosing the service to receiving the resulting report, without promising an outcome that depends on the actual installation. Short headings and compact sections reduce the amount of technical language visitors must process at once. On mobile, the same service order remains visible. The portfolio entry explains Enspect's real inspection workflow instead of using a generic engineering-site formula.
